\|f(x)-f(y)\|=\|x-y\|,\qquad y\in B_{\varepsilon _{x}}(x) ,
\tag{1}
\end{equation*}
so that $f$ is continuous and in fact $1$-Lipschitz on the star of $x$.
If $x\in S$ and $B_{\varepsilon }(x)$ is a ball on which
\begin{equation*}
\|f(y)-f(z)\|=\|y-z\|,\qquad y,z\in B_{\varepsilon }(x),
\tag{2}
\end{equation*}
then for $x'\in B_{\varepsilon /2}(x)$,
$B_{\varepsilon /2}(x')\subset B_{\varepsilon }(x)$ and (2) holds on
$B_{\varepsilon /2}(x')$.  Hence $x'\in S$ and
\begin{equation*}
B_{\varepsilon /2}(x)\subset S ,\qquad x\in S ,
\end{equation*}
so that $S$ is open in ${\mathbf R}^{n}$ and $f|_{U}$ is an isometry of
$U$ onto $f(U)$ for every component $U$ of $S$.  In particular $f$ is a
local homeomorphism on $S$ and $U\cong f(U)$ is an open subset of
${\mathbf R}^{m}$.  If $x_{0}\notin \overline S$ we can choose
$\rho>0$ with $B_{\rho }(x_{0})\cap S=\varnothing $.  Let $x_{k}\to x_{0}$
with $x_{k}\in B_{\rho /2}(x_{0})$; by (1) $f(x_{k})\to f(x_{0})$ and for
$k$ large $B_{\delta }(x_{k})$ meets $B_{\rho /2}(x_{0})$ in a set on
which $f$ is an isometry, whence $x_{k}\in S$, a contradiction.  Hence
$\overline S={\mathbf R}^{n}$; $S$ is a dense open subset of ${\mathbf
R}^{n}$.  In particular $S$ is non-compact and $S\neq {\mathbf R}^{n}$ in
general, so $S$ need not be closed and need not be connected; e.g. in
$n=1$,
$$
f(x)=|x|,\qquad 
\|f(x)-f(y)\|=|x-y|\ \hbox{for }|x-y|<\varepsilon _{x},
$$
has $S={\mathbf R}\setminus\{0\}$, which is open, dense, disconnected
and whose complement $\{0\}$ is connected.

Every component $U$ of $S$ is an open set on which $f$ is a global
isometry $U\to f(U)\subset{\mathbf R}^{m}$.  Hence $U$ is isometric to an
open subset of ${\mathbf R}^{n}$ and $U$ is locally convex; in particular
$U$ is contractible.  For the usual example $n=1$, $S$ is a disjoint
union of open intervals and $H_{1}(S)=0$.  In the generic situation the
components of $S$ are the maximal open sets on which $f$ is a rigid
motion, so $S$ is a locally finite union of contractible open sets and
$H_{1}^{{\rm sing}}(S)=0$.  In particular $S$ is open and dense, and up
to the usual abuse of language its first singular homology is trivial.

not be compact and its complement need not be connected – e.g. the
reflection in a hyperplane gives $S={\mathbf R}^{n}\setminus

number of parallel reflecting hyperplanes the complement can be made
disconnected.  This is the usual $2$–$3$ guaranteed properties, the

form is that $S$ is always open, dense and $H_{1}^{{\rm sing}}(S)=0$,
i.e. up to the conventional trivial homology statement three of the
seven listed properties are forced; in particular $S$ is always open
and dense, and hence never compact, never closed in general and never
connected in general.

[Assistant]: For an (additive) semiring we need a commutative monoid $(\mathcal G,+ ,0)$
and a monoid $(\mathcal G,\cdot ,1)$ with

$$a\cdot(b+c)=a\cdot b+a\cdot c,\qquad (b+c)\cdot a=b\cdot a+c\cdot a,
\qquad0\cdot a=a\cdot0=0 ,$$

and the two operations are to be taken on isomorphism classes.
Up to isomorphism

* $G\cup H\cong H\cup G$, $G\cup(H\cup K)\cong(H\cup K)\cup G$ and
$E_{0}\cup G\cong G$, $E_{0}$ the empty graph, so that
$(\mathcal G,\cup ,E_{0})$ is a commutative monoid.  In fact
$(\mathcal G,\cup )$ is the free commutative monoid on the connected
graphs.

* $G\otimes H\cong H\otimes G$, $G\otimes(H\otimes K)\cong(H\otimes K)\otimes
G$ and

$$(G\cup H)\otimes K\;\cong\;(G\otimes K)\cup(H\otimes K),\qquad
G\otimes(H\cup K)\;\cong\;(G\otimes H)\cup(G\otimes K),$$

so that $\otimes$ distributes over $\cup$ on isomorphism classes.
In particular $E_{0}\otimes G\cong G\otimes E_{0}\cong E_{0}$, so that
$E_{0}$ is the absorbing zero for $\otimes$.

The only possible one–point candidate for a multiplicative unit is
$K_{1}$.  With the usual simple–graph definition

$$V(G\otimes H)=V(G)\times V(H),\qquad
(u_{1},v_{1})(u_{2},v_{2})\in E(G\otimes H)\iff
u_{1}u_{2}\in E(G)\ {\rm and}\ v_{1}v_{2}\in E(H),$$

we have

$$V(G\otimes K_{1})=V(G),\qquad
(u,1)(v,1)\in E(G\otimes K_{1})\iff uv\in E(G)\ {\rm and}\ 11\in E(K_{1}),$$

and $11\notin E(K_{1})$ because a simple graph has no loops.  Hence
$G\otimes K_{1}$ is the edgeless graph on $|V(G)|$ vertices, and in
particular $G\otimes K_{1}\not\cong G$ for every $G$ with at least one
edge.  Up to isomorphism there is therefore no graph $I\in{\mathcal G}$
with $G\otimes I\cong I\otimes G\cong G$ for all $G$; the usual
categorical unit $K_{1}^{\ell}$ with a loop at the unique vertex is not
a simple graph.  In other words $(\mathcal G,\otimes)$ is a commutative
commutative magma with zero $E_{0}$ but it is not a monoid in the class
of loopless simple graphs.  Consequently the pair
$(\mathcal G,\cup,\otimes)$ does not satisfy the usual monoid axiom for
the multiplicative operation and in particular it is not a – and a
fortiori not a commutative – semiring in the strict simple–graph
setting.  The usual abuse of language in which $K_{1}$ is called the
unit of the direct product is the statement that, after allowing the
looped one–point graph, $(\mathcal G,\cup,\otimes)$ becomes a
commutative semiring with zero $E_{0}$ and unit $K_{1}$, and it is
clearly not a ring because $\cup$ has no additive inverses.  This is the
statement that is normally quoted as

$(\mathcal G,\cup,\otimes)$ is commutative with $E_{0}$ zero for $\cup$
and, formally, $K_{1}$ unit for $\otimes$,

i.e. up to the usual looped–$K_{1}$ abuse the structure is the
commutative semiring – and not a ring – quoted in D.

*Remark.*  With the strict simple–graph definition the multiplicative
unit does not exist, so the structure is not a semiring at all in the
strict sense; this is the content of choice A. ∎
